cases.question: Our Singapore-incorporated private company changed its business email ten days ago. Can the secretary wait until the next annual return to tell ACRA?
expected: The email change must be filed with ACRA within 14 days from the change.
The annual return does not replace the change notification.
forbidden: A 30-day deadline for this local company.
Permission to wait until the annual return.

cases.question: We are an overseas-incorporated company registered in Singapore as a foreign company. We changed our registered office twenty days ago. A colleague says every ACRA entity has only fourteen days. Are we already late?
expected: Foreign companies have 30 days from the change.
At twenty days, the stated notification deadline has not yet expired.
The general 14-day period has a foreign-company exception.
forbidden: An unconditional conclusion that the company is already late.
No notification obligation for foreign companies.

cases.question: Our company has a September year-end. Its accounts for the year ended 30/09/2024 relate to YA 2025, and the tax return has been filed. Can we shred the supporting invoices on 01/10/2029?
expected: No: retention is at least five years from the relevant YA.
For YA 2025, retain through at least 31/12/2029.
Completed filing does not end the retention obligation.
forbidden: Five years measured only from the financial year-end.
Permission to destroy the invoices on 01/10/2029.

cases.question: A company was struck off and dissolved on 15/08/2026. Its former director thinks the old YA retention periods have expired, so nobody needs to keep its books now. Is that right, and would responsibility differ if it had been wound up?
expected: For a struck-off and dissolved company, a person who was an officer immediately before dissolution must ensure retention.
Books and papers must be retained for at least five years after dissolution.
For winding up, the liquidator bears the stated duty, with at least five years from dissolution.
forbidden: Immediate disposal because old YA periods expired.
Treating winding-up commencement as the dissolution-date anchor.

cases.question: We found an ordinary CPF overpayment on 01/10/2026. The payment record says PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON 06/11/2025. Do we have a year from discovering the mistake to request our money back?
expected: Apply immediately, no later than one year from contribution payment.
The recorded received date determines that payment date.
The outer deadline is 06/11/2026, rather than October 2027.
forbidden: A fresh one-year period from discovery.
A guarantee that the entire amount will be refunded.

cases.question: CPF was paid on a conditional joining bonus in 2024. Under the employment terms, the employee had to repay the bonus on 15/09/2026. We are applying in October 2026. Is the claim too old, and can we wait for CPF Board's refund before returning the employee's contribution share?
expected: The conditional-wage clock runs from the date wages were supposed to be repaid.
Apply immediately and no later than 15/09/2027; indicate that repayment-due date.
Return the applicable employee share directly before submitting the application.
forbidden: Rejecting timing solely because contributions were paid in 2024.
Using actual eventual repayment instead of the contractual or agreed due date.
Returning the employee share only after CPF Board pays the employer.

cases.question: For staff covered by the Employment Act, our bank salary transfer succeeds but the payroll portal cannot generate the itemised statement that day. How long can we take to provide it, and may we email it?
expected: Normally provide the payslip together with payment.
If unable, provide it within three working days of payment.
An electronic payslip is permitted.
forbidden: A general seven-day allowance.
Treating the fallback as three calendar days.
Requiring paper only.

cases.question: We dismissed an employee covered by the Employment Act and are now paying the outstanding salary. Payroll wants to send the itemised payslip three working days later under the usual fallback. Is that acceptable?
expected: For termination or dismissal, provide the payslip together with outstanding salary.
The ordinary delayed-payslip fallback does not justify this proposed delay.
forbidden: Allowing three working days after the outstanding salary payment.
Substituting only the general final-salary payment deadline for the payslip answer.

cases.question: Our licensed fund management company has selected a new chief executive. Can she start first if we tell MAS about the appointment within fourteen days, or is there a form and approval needed beforehand?
expected: Obtain MAS approval before the CEO appointment.
Use Form 11 for the appointment.
A post-appointment notification is insufficient.
forbidden: Permission to appoint first and notify within fourteen days.
Treating submission of Form 11 alone as approval.

cases.question: At our LFMC, an existing non-executive director will take an executive role. Since he is already on the board, can we simply notify MAS afterwards? Would moving an executive director into a non-executive role follow the same process?
expected: Non-executive to executive requires prior MAS approval through Form 11.
Existing board membership does not remove that requirement.
Executive to non-executive is a notification under Notice of Change in Particulars, as soon as practicable.
forbidden: Treating both directions as post-change notifications.
Applying the resignation-specific fourteen-day deadline universally.
Treating both directions as requiring Form 11 prior approval.
